//: Tags match the four already in the repo (search-0.1.5, netgrep-0.1.5): component included, no `v`. release-please would otherwise write search-v0.2.0 next to search-0.1.5.
//separate-pull-requests: One PR covering every component. Three PRs would have to be merged in dependency order by hand, which is the ordering problem release.yml exists to remove.
//bump-minor-pre-major: A breaking change gives 0.3.0, not 1.0.0. 1.0.0 is a claim this project does not make by accident — reaching it needs an explicit `Release-As: 1.0.0` footer.

packages/search.//: Cargo.toml is the source of truth, but scripts/verify-pack.mjs fails the build when it disagrees with the npm wrapper — and post_build.js, which normally syncs them, does not run in CI's `bundle` job. So both must move in the same commit.
packages/search.//Cargo.lock: The Rust updater only looks for a lock inside the package directory; this workspace keeps one at the root. Without this entry Cargo.toml moves and the lock does not, and cargo silently rewrites it on the next build.

packages/example.//: Private and never published. It is a component so that a demo-only change produces a release, which is what triggers the Pages deploy — without one the live site would freeze until a library change happened along. Its version means `which build of the site`, nothing more.
packages/example.//initial-version: There is no example-* tag, so this is a first release — and release-please's default first version is 1.0.0, which would put the demo a major ahead of the library it demonstrates.

//plugins: @netgrep/netgrep depends on @netgrep/search via `workspace:*`, which pnpm rewrites to an EXACT version at pack time — so a search release nobody pairs with a netgrep release reaches no consumer. Locking the two versions together makes that pin correct by construction. The cost is a no-op republish of one package when only the other changed.
